full_judgment:
2. The plaintiff-opposite party instituted the Money Suit against the defendant petitioner for recovery of a sum of Rs.62,828/29 paisa alleging that the defendant secured two contract works for construction of Terminal Buildings of Inland Water Transport Authority, hereinafter referred to as I.W.T.A. at Bhola Motor Launch Station and at Ilshaghat and obtained financial assistance from the plaintiff in connection with the said contract works and the present suit has been filed for recovery of the same due from the defendant petitioner in respect of the money advanced by the plaintiff to him. After the filing of the suit at Barisal Court the plaintiff opposite-party filed an application for attachment before judgment of some immovable properties alleged to be belonging to the defendant as well as the money due to the defendant from the I.W.T.A. and a conditional order of attachment was passed by the Subordinate Judge on 28-11-68 which was made absolute on 19-1-72. As against this order of attachment before judgment an appeal was filed before the High Court of Bangladesh being F.M.A. No.6 of 1972 which was allowed by the High Court on 1-6-72 and the order of attachment was set aside. Thereafter it appears, the plaintiff-opposite party instituted a suit being Title Suit No.49 of 1972 in the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge at Dhaka impleading the I.W.T.A. and the Uttara Bank, Dilkusha Branch as defendants 1 and 2 and the petitioner as defendant No.3 praying that a decree declaring that the plaintiff has a lien on the sum due by defendant No.1 to the defendant No.3 in respect of the contract works of Ilsha ghat and Bhola Motor Launch Terminal Buildings be passed. After the records of Money Suit No.9 of 1968 have been received by the learned Subordinator Judge at Barisal on 22-6-72 after the disposal of the First Miscellaneous Appeal by the High Court, the learned Subordinate Judge on a fresh application made by the plaintiff-opposite party under Order 38, rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure passed another order of attachment before judgment of the immovable properties as well as money due from IWTA, as mentioned in the petition on 1-7-72 and directed notice to issue upon the defendant to show cause why he should not furnish security for Rs.66,700/-. The learned Subordinate Judge by his order dated 25-1-72 confirmed the conditional order of attachment in respect of the money owed to the defendant by the IWTA Authority and vacated the order of attachment so far as the immovable properties were concerned. As against this order defendant again filed an appeal before the Bangladesh High Court being F.M.A. No. 37 of 1972 which was allowed by the High Court by its judgment and order dated 24-8-72 and the order of attachment before judgment was set aside. 

 6. Mr. Abdul Hye Chowdhury has very seriously contended that if the suit is not tried at Dacca his client will be deprived of the benefit of the evidence of IWTA officials which, according to him, is very important for the purpose of proving his client's case and the object of securing the evidence of the said officials residing at Dacca would be a sufficient ground for transfer of the suit to Dacca. When it was pointed out to Mr. Abdul Hye Chowdhury that the difficulty or inconvenience of examining two or three witnesses of a particular party, who live beyond the territorial jurisdiction of the court had never been regarded as sufficient ground for transfer of a suit from one jurisdiction to another. Mr. Hye Chowdhury cited three decisions in support of his contention. In considering the question whether a suit should be transferred from one court to another, it has been held in a number of decisions that the question of conveniences of both the parties may be one of the grounds of the transfer of a suit from one court to another. But the facility for examining some of the witnesses of one party alone has hardly ever been considered to be a good ground for transfer of a case from one jurisdiction to another. The plaintiff has a right to choose his own forum and therefore a suit should not be transferred to another court unless some very strong grounds have been made out in this behalf The decisions which have been cited on behalf of Mr. Abdul Hye Chowdhury go to support this proposition. The first citation is that of IIR 9 Calcutta 980 (Khatija Bibi Vs. Tarok Chander Dutt), in which Chief Justice Garth laid down balance of convenience or expense as one of the criteria for a transfer of a suit and observed as follows:- 

 "Prima facie, the plaintiff as the abiter litis has a right to bring his suit in any Court which the law allows: and s.23 is only intended as we consider, to provide for those cases, where, on the ground of expense or convenience, or some other good reason, the Court thinks that the place of trial ought to be changed. 

 "The jurisdiction of a superior Court to transfer a suit from one subordinate Court to another ought to Ix exercised with extreme caution. The choice of forum given to a plaintiff by the Legislature ought not to be lightly interfered with, and the Court will not transfer a suit properly laid except Upon proof of special circumstances. A well recognised ground exists when the convenience of necessary witnesses and the ends of justice will be promoted by the transfer but the ground alleged must be clearly established." 

 9. In this case the only ground suggested by Mr. Abdul Hye Choudhury is that the testimony of some of the witnesses who reside at Dacca, i e., certain officials of IWTA may not be available for the purpose of the defendant's case. Now, the plaintiff's suit is based on certain transactions which are alleged to have been taken place at places within the district of Barisal and most of the witnesses who are likely to be examined in this case are residents of those places. The learned Advocate for the opposite party has pointed out that the plaintiff-opposite party has, as a matter of fact, cited as many as 19 witnesses all of whom are residents either of Barisal Town or of Bhola and other neighbouring places. The defendant, of course, has not cited any witness as yet but apart from IWTA officials to whom reference has been made by the learned Advocate for the petitioner in course of his argument, no other witness, who may be examined on his behalf has been alleged to be resident at any place near about Dacca. It is also extremely doubtful if the evidence of these IWTA officials will at all be necessary for the purpose of the defence case. Neither in the plaint of the Money Suit nor in the written statement filed therein,  any reference has been made to these officials. If, however, the evidence of these persons is considered necessary by the defendant there are sufficient provisions in the Code of Civil Procedure to make their evidence available to the court. It is not the convenience of one party but it is the balance of convenience of the parties which is a criterion for exercising the power for transfer of a suit. We do not therefore find any substance in the contention of Mr. Abdul Hye Chowdhury in this regard. 

 13. Now in this case an order confirming a conditional order of attachment before judgment was passed by the learned Subordinate Judge which was set aside by a Division Bench of Bangladesh High Court. The judgment of the High Court dealt at some length with the law relating to attachment of properties before judgment and pointed out the necessary condition which could have been satisfied before such a power was exercised. It was specifically stressed in the said judgment that it was an extraordinary power, which should be used with utmost caution and should be sparingly exercised. After the delivery of this judgment of the High Court, the records were received in the Court of Subordinate Judge on 22-6-72, and on 29-6-72 a fresh application was filed on behalf of the plaintiff under Order 38, rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure. On this application the learned Subordinate Judge passed an ex parte order on the 1st of July, 1972 attaching the self-same properties as were the subject-matter of attachment on the previous occasion. The learned Subordinate Judge did not appear to pay much attention to the judgment of the High Court incoming to the following conclusion : 

 14. The defendant subsequently appeared and the matter was finally heard on 29-7-72. By his judgment passed on the same day the learned Subordinate Judge confirmed the previous order so far as the bail money and the security money payable by the IWTA were concerned but the order relating to the immovable properties, none of which was claimed by the defendant, was vacated on the ground that the order regarding the said properties could not be sustained in view of the judgment of the High Court. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has drawn our attention to the manner in which the learned Subordinate Judge has dealt in this judgment with the argument of the defendant relating to the observance of the rules for swearing affidavits as provided in Order 19 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It appears that when in the argument advanced on behalf of the defendant the question was raised as to the regularity of the affidavits on the basis of which the order for attachment before judgment was passed, the learned Subordinate Judge, instead of going into the merits of this argument, brushed it aside by pointing out the defects in the affidavits of the defendant himself. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has submitted that the supposed defect, as pointed out by the learned Subordinate Judge, was certain statements made by the defendant about the plaintiffs dilatory tactics and conduct in delaying the hearing of the attachment matter. According to the learned Subordinate Judge, it was the defendant alone, and not the plaintiff at all, who was responsible for taking adjournments from time to time and delaying the hearing of the attachment matter. But the petitioner has quoted certain orders in his application from the order-sheet to show that the plaintiff took several adjournments from  25-10-71 to 7-12-71 while the defendant insisting on the hearing of the matter, Mr. Khandkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the opposite party, however, submitted that it was true that during the latter part of the proceeding the plaintiff took some adjournments for a brief period but at the earlier stage it was the defendant who took adjournments. 

 15. It seems to us, however, that the main question is not whether the plaintiff or the defendant took to dilatory tactics for delaying the hearing of the proceeding in question, and the defendant made some untrue statements in his affidavit in this regard, but is, whether the learned Subordinate Judge has been able to maintain the necessary judicial poise and equanimity in dealing with the respective case of the parties and has acted judicially in disposing of the matters before him. The learned Subordinate Judge may have been, to some extent, irritated when the defendant who; according to the learned Subordinate Judge was himself responsible for delaying the proceeding, was trying to complain against the plaintiff for delaying the same. But even if his view about the defendant's conduct was correct which does not appear from the records to be wholly correct his failure to deal with the question raised on behalf of the defendant, which was patently necessary for a proper determination of the question before him, does not give an account of his fair-minded approach to the said question. As a matter of fact, the High Court pointed out in its judgment in F.M.A.37 of 1972 the learned Subordinate Judge was not at all mindful about the instructions given by the High Court in the Manual of Practical Instructions for the guidance of subordinate civil courts in regard to the applications under Order 38 of the Code and that the affidavits filed on behalf of the plaintiff sere inadequate and defective, and should not have been the basis for issuing an order of attachment.
